Verified and named the pending reauthorization bill: Improve and Enhance the Work Opportunity Tax Credit Act (S. 3265), a five-year extension through 2030.

advisor.summary: The §51 Work Opportunity Tax Credit pays employers for hiring from targeted groups — veterans, SNAP recipients, the long-term unemployed, ex-felons, vocational-rehab referrals, and others — generally 40% of the first $6,000 of first-year wages ($2,400 per hire), rising to $9,600 for certain disabled veterans and up to $9,000 over two years for long-term family assistance hires. Process carries the entire benefit: Form 8850 pre-screening signed by the offer date and filed with the state workforce agency within 28 calendar days of the start date, with no reasonable-cause relief for a miss. The 2026 complication is authorization: the statutory hiring deadline was December 31, 2025, and as of mid-2026 the credit sits in a lapse pending reauthorization (the bipartisan Improve and Enhance the Work Opportunity Tax Credit Act, S. 3265, would extend the credit five years through 2030), with agencies logging but not certifying 2026-start applications. The historical practice — screen and file through every hiatus, because renewals have been retroactive — is the professional standard, and it is how this engagement runs. The engine applies 40% to the entered certified wages; the caps, hour tiers, and §280C(a) wage-deduction reduction are handled in the input and at the return.
mechanics: The credit equals 40% of qualified first-year wages when the certified employee works at least 400 hours, 25% at 120–399 hours, and nothing below 120 hours; the engine multiplies the entered certified-wage figure by 40%, so the input must already embed the correct tier and the per-group wage caps.

Wage caps run by group under §51: generally $6,000 (a $2,400 maximum), up to $24,000 for certain qualified veterans (a $9,600 maximum), $3,000 for summer youth, and a two-year structure worth up to $9,000 for long-term family assistance recipients under §51(e).

Certification is the credit: §51(d)(13) requires Form 8850, signed by both employer and applicant on or before the job-offer date, filed with the state workforce agency within 28 calendar days after the start date, together with ETA Form 9061 or 9062 — self-attestation without agency certification claims nothing.

Statutory authorization covered hires beginning work by December 31, 2025 under P.L. 116-260; for 2026 start dates the program sits in lapse pending reauthorization, state agencies are accepting but holding applications, and the discipline is to keep screening and filing so retroactive renewal — the historical pattern — captures the pipeline.

§280C(a) trims the employer's wage deduction by the credit claimed, the same wages cannot support overlapping employment credits, and the credit flows through Form 5884 into the §38 general business credit with §39 carryovers.

Pre-screening and certification mechanics — Form 8850 to the state workforce agency within 28 days of the start date, the deadline that decides most claims.
The two-year structure, worth up to $9,000, for long-term family assistance hires.
Reduces the wage deduction by the credit — the no-double-benefit adjustment carried on the return.

requirements: New hires certified by the state workforce agency as targeted-group members — rehires and §51(i) related parties do not qualify.
Form 8850 signed by the offer date and filed within 28 calendar days of each start date, built into onboarding so no eligible hire slips through.
Hours tracked to the 120- and 400-hour thresholds, with first-year qualified wages isolated in payroll for each certified employee.
For 2026-start hires: the client's written acknowledgment that the credit is contingent on congressional reauthorization.
risks: Authorization is the front-of-mind risk: the statute lapsed for hires beginning work after December 31, 2025, and although renewals have historically been retroactive, a 2026-start credit cannot be treated as earned until Congress acts — model it as contingent and say so in the plan.
The 28-day Form 8850 window is the leading cause of lost credits in ordinary times; no reasonable-cause relief exists, so the screening process must live inside onboarding, not in the tax file.
Certifications routinely take months, pushing credits onto amended returns or holding them past the original filing — set that expectation early.
Omitting the §280C(a) wage-deduction reduction, or counting the same wages toward other employment credits, are the recurring return-level errors.
The credit is nonrefundable; low-liability years strand it in a carryforward the model does not track.
stateNotes: Conformity: the credit is federal-only, but states conforming to federal taxable income — Missouri among them through its federal starting point — inherit the smaller wage deduction §280C(a) leaves behind.
PTET interaction: none directly; the credit flows to owners federally, while the slightly higher entity income from the reduced wage deduction feeds any pass-through entity tax base.

Missouri: no state piggyback WOTC exists, so the federal credit is the entire benefit; Missouri hires are certified through the state's workforce agency (the Division of Employment Security intake for WOTC), and the 28-day clock runs from each Missouri start date like anywhere else.
reviewChecklist: Screening embedded in onboarding — Form 8850 page one at application or offer, page two at hire — with a per-hire 28-day calendar in place.
Certified wages in the model reflect agency certifications on hand, correct hour tiers, and per-group caps — never projected or self-attested eligibility.
2026-start hires flagged as authorization-contingent in the client deliverable.
§280C(a) reduction and the no-overlap check completed on the return claiming Form 5884.
Certification-pending hires tracked toward amended-return or carryover treatment.

client.teaser: People you already hire may earn you a tax credit — if a short form is filed within 28 days.
client.headline: Turn your everyday hiring into tax credits
plainEnglish: The government rewards employers who hire people who face barriers to work. That includes veterans, people out of work a long time, and people on certain assistance programs. The reward is a credit — usually $2,400 per qualifying hire, and up to $9,600 for some veterans.

Many employers make hires that qualify and never collect a dime. The rule is strict: a short screening form must reach the state within 28 days of the start date. Miss that window and the credit is gone for good.

One honest caveat right now: Congress let this program lapse at the end of 2025 and is working on a renewal. Past renewals have almost always been backdated. So we keep screening and filing for every hire — that way, when the renewal comes, your credits are already in line.
client.analogy: Think of it as a rebate slip attached to certain new hires — worth real money, but only if it goes out within 28 days of their first day.
